newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal budget set for first parliamentary test.
newsitem.headline: Portugal budget set for first parliamentary test.

text.p: Portugal's minority Socialist government will put its plan to secure a place in monetary union to the test on Wednesday when parliament starts to debate the 1997 budget.

The budget is crucial to Portugal's chances of qualifying for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the government has warned that it may seek fresh elections rather than see the blueprint significantly changed by the legislature.
But with its main opponents, the centre-right Social Democrats (PSD), as committed to Europe as the Socialists, economists and political analysts see little chance of a parliamentary showdown.
Deputy PSD leader in parliament Manuela Ferreira Leite told a news conference on Monday that the opposition saw it as "essential" that the budget "put Portugal in monetary union."

The Socialists are four seats short of an outright majority in the 230-seat parliament but only the Communist Party and the right-wing Popular Party, which together muster 30 seats, are openly hostile to Portugal's EMU pretensions.
"It is very, very improbable that the budget will not be approved (in parliament)," Banco Finantia chief economist Joao Morais told Reuters.

But despite agreeing with the government on the need for a deficit-cutting budget to meet one of the main entry tests for monetary union, due to be launched in 1999, the Social Democrats have strongly criticised some measures in the package.
But Ferreira Leite has indicated that the party, which has 88 parliamentary seats, would hold its fire until the budget is voted on, clause-by-clause, in early December.
This week's initial debate will end with a vote on Friday on the budget's principles and aims. More detailed srutiny will be left until next month ahead of a final vote on December 11.
The government has forecast a budget deficit next year of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), just inside the three percent ceiling set for entry to EMU.

With progress on reducing the gap between state spending and income already made in 1996, when the deficit is projected at around four percent compared with five percent in 1995, few economists predict problems with meeting the single currency deficit goal.
Inflation, which Portugal needs to cut to below three percent from 3.4 percent currently, is widely viewed as posing the stiffest challenge.
"The deficit target is viewed as being credible by the markets. It must be, otherwise there would be no explanation for how interest rates have been falling," said Morais.

As with Spain and Italy, two other countries long considered unlikely contenders for the single currency, Portugal's interest rates have dropped sharply as investors begin to view it as a serious candidate.
But critics say the government's budget plan relies too heavily on boosting income through more efficient tax gathering than on reducing state spending.
Over half of the 1.1 percentage point reduction in the deficit next year will come from higher tax revenues, including a crackdown on tax dodging.

Neverthless, independent economists say the government has a safety net if the rise in revenues looks like failing to meet expectations. It has budgetted for a 13 percent increase in public sector investment next year and it would be a simple matter to slow such spending, they say.
